extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary fiction / general readers (18th‑century travel/epistolary novel audience)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from an epistolary travel‑novel (letters) offering descriptive narrative and the speaker’s evaluative opinions about language, manners, institutions, and society. The text mixes travel reporting with argumentative assertions about pronunciation, politics, and law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of speech: Edinburgh vs London
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that 'the English language was spoken with greater propriety at Edinburgh than in London.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the Scottish dialect is 'true, genuine old English' with some French terms; modern English has been weakened by affectation and false refinement. Examples given: Scots retain pronunciations that make Chaucer, Spenser, and Shakespeare more intelligible to them than to South Britons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of ancient forms preserves meaning and intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Retaining older meanings and pronunciations preserves sense that modern speakers have lost; e.g. the Tempest line 'He’s gentle and not fearful' originally meant 'noble/high‑minded' rather than 'timid'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Spenser's 'A gentle knight...' where 'gentle' aligns with being high‑spirited; Scots would express similar sentiments in nearly the same terms. Implication: preserving archaic usage aids interpretation of older poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'false refinement' that corrupts language energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that modern English has 'weakened, and even corrupted' language by throwing out guttural sounds, altering pronunciation and quantity, and disusing many significant words and terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: words pronounced identically in modern English but distinct among Scots (wright, write, right, rite); vowels altered from continental norms; many vowels treated as diphthongs (i and u). The result is difficulty for foreigners and loss of expressive energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation clarity aids foreign comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that a foreigner who 'understood English tolerably well' might still need a Scotchman to explain what an English native said, because Scots enunciate more clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: Scots (and Swiss speaking French) speak the words without the native 'music' or recitative, making individual words clearer to learners. Clear articulation and not 'mumbling' improves intelligibility to non‑native speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language 'recitative' (music) matters and must be learned
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed principle: every language has a peculiar recitative or music which must be acquired alongside words; the music is essential to native speech but makes acquisition harder for learners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: a Parisian's recitative makes French harder for foreigners than the Swiss who 'speak the words only'. Implication for learners: both vocabulary and rhythm/cadence must be learned for true fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce tends to moral corruption and national ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that commerce, when it flourishes, will sooner or later prove the ruin of every nation where it thrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: sudden affluence from trade opens sluices of luxury leading to profligacy, corruption of manners, bankruptcy and ruin; commerce's rise resembles a tide that once ebbed will not return to former heights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary venality undermines constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that the parliament is the 'rotten part of the British constitution' because of buying boroughs and canvassing for votes, establishing venality over principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences argued: a venal parliament is corruptible by the crown's patronage (posts, pensions), can lengthen its own authority, and combined with a standing army can enable ambitious sovereigns to overthrow constitutional bulwarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press is dangerous without proper restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: View that the liberty of the press is 'a national evil' while it enables base persons to soil merit and incendiaries to disturb public peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: the author admits the press can be valuable under due restrictions, but claims there is 'no law in England sufficient to restrain it within proper bounds' at present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimous jury requirement produces perjury and injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that juries composed of illiterate plebeians, coupled with the requirement of unanimity, lead to perjury and unjust verdicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics: if one juror is bribed or bent, he can hold out until others are 'fatigued and starved into concurrence', forcing false verdicts. Alternatives praised: Sweden (simple majority) and Scotland (two‑thirds) avoid this absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferment favors money, connexions, and partiality over merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that, in competition for positions, natives of England have advantages (partiality, connections, parliamentary interest, money) that favor their preferment over Scots, regardless of equal merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: Scots frequently must 'purchase' advancement (with money or recruits) to rise above lower ranks in the army, whereas natives of South‑Britain more often succeed without such purchases.
